Function-to-taxon visualizations

function-to-taxon.Rmd

Use this guide to adjust figures after the function-centered analysis. It reuses that study’s fitted results and inputs rather than creating another example analysis.

The example selects candidate KOs and retains all fitted class contributors, including Alphaproteobacteria and Candidatus_Peribacteria. It does not inherit the taxon-centered exclusions.

Keep ps, fun_strat_path, study_tree, result_fun, result_fun_box, ko_candidates, group_col, the group contrast and output directory from the study. Select a small set of functions before creating any plot.

Select functions before plotting

Choose a few functions before creating any function-to-taxon diagram. The source table contains 8,881 KOs; the demonstration fits a biologically motivated set of 24 rather than drawing the full library. Keep the full result saved and make a smaller plotting list. The code below preserves the recorded analysis settings.

available_functions <- names(result_fun)[vapply(result_fun, nrow, integer(1)) > 0L]
functions_of_interest <- intersect(ko_candidates, available_functions)
# Replace the selection with named KOs of interest when they are available.
# functions_of_interest <- c("K01489", "K00432")
stopifnot(length(functions_of_interest) > 0L,
          all(functions_of_interest %in% names(result_fun)))
result_fun_plot <- result_fun[functions_of_interest]
attr(result_fun_plot, "microfun") <- attr(result_fun, "microfun")
selected_function <- if ("K01489" %in% functions_of_interest) "K01489" else functions_of_interest[1]
stopifnot(selected_function %in% functions_of_interest)

All examples below use this filtered list. To fit the real study results first, follow the function-centered analysis, which fits the 24 selected candidate KOs at Class level. The full 8,881-KO library is a separate, much longer option.

Sankey

Use this overview to see which taxa are linked to each selected function. Keeping individual KOs visible makes it easier to follow a specific feature; grouping functions can be useful for a broader summary. Decide which resolution you want before interpreting a visually large group of links.

Functions appear on the left and taxa on the right. Set group_functions = FALSE to retain individual KOs. Optional taxonomy or ASV phylogeny appears on the taxon side.

p_fun_phylogeny <- fun2tax_sankey(
  result_fun_plot, pathway = "KO", group_functions = FALSE,
  tree_mode = "phylogeny", physeq = ps, phylo_tree = study_tree
)
save_sankey(p_fun_phylogeny, file.path(out, "fun2tax_sankey.html"))

Chord

Use Chord to compare the predicted contributions behind the selected relationships. A broad ribbon identifies a large mean contribution in the plotted subset, while the outer bar describes the absolute modeled effect.

Inspect the selected functions in HTML first. A dense full PDF can load slowly, so choose an interesting function, regenerate a smaller diagram and export that selection to PDF.

The contribution weighting, effect colours, taxonomy bands and export interfaces match the taxon-to-function Chord. Use function-oriented results and select relevant function IDs.

p_fun_chord <- fun2tax_chord(
  result_fun_plot, fun_strat_path, ps, group = group_col,
  contrast = c(reference, target), functions = functions_of_interest,
  draw = FALSE
)
save_chord(p_fun_chord, file.path(out, "fun2tax_chord.html"))

# After inspecting HTML, select one function for a focused PDF.
p_fun_focus <- fun2tax_chord(
  result_fun_plot, fun_strat_path, ps, group = group_col,
  contrast = c(reference, target), functions = selected_function,
  max_taxa_per_function = 5, draw = FALSE
)
save_chord(p_fun_focus, file.path(out, "fun2tax_chord_focus.html"))
save_chord(p_fun_focus, file.path(out, "fun2tax_chord_focus.pdf"))

Contribution boxplots

For a selected function, compare how different taxa contribute across sample groups. Look for the spread and overlap as well as the medians. The log-transformed y-axis helps show contributions on different scales; equal visual distances on that axis are not equal changes in the original contribution units.

An ungrouped call returns one named plot per function. The y-axis is log10(contribution + 1e-6).

result_fun_box <- result_fun_plot[selected_function]
z <- result_fun_box[[selected_function]]
result_fun_box[[selected_function]] <- head(z[order(z$p_adjust), , drop = FALSE], 5L)
attr(result_fun_box, "microfun") <- attr(result_fun_plot, "microfun")
fun_boxes <- fun2tax_box(
  fun_strat_path, result_fun_box, ps, group = group_col,
  pathway = "KO", group_functions = FALSE
)
p_fun_box <- fun_boxes[[selected_function]]
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "fun2tax_box.pdf"), p_fun_box,
                width = 9, height = 6)

Association dendrogram

Here the function defines a branch and its contributing taxa define the leaves. This view is useful for comparing which taxa appear among the selected model effects for several functions. It is an association summary, so do not read it as a phylogenetic tree or a clustering of taxon abundance profiles.

Functions label branches, and contributing taxa label the leaves. top_n_per_function controls how many taxa are displayed per function.

p_fun_dendro <- fun2tax_dendro(
  result_fun_plot, top_n_per_function = 3, label_size = 2.6,
  wrap_width = 20
)$plot
p_fun_dendro <- p_fun_dendro +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.6, 1.6), ylim = c(-1.6, 1.6), clip = "off")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "fun2tax_dendrogram.pdf"), p_fun_dendro,
                width = 10, height = 7.5)

Signed model effects

A signed-effect plot brings the contrast into focus. Which taxa have positive effects for the selected function, and which have negative effects? Read the model scale and reference group before comparing bar lengths, then compare the selected taxa.

fun_effects <- fun2tax_logfc(result_fun_plot, top_n = 3)
p_fun_effect <- fun_effects[[selected_function]] +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "MaAsLin2 AST coefficient")
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(out, "fun2tax_effect.pdf"), p_fun_effect,
                width = 8, height = 5)

Choose names from names(result_fun) and record the reference/target contrast. The axis label records the model estimate used by the fitted backend.

When you return to the community-level result

A function may change overall because a few contributors shift strongly or because many shift together. It may also remain similar in total while its contributors change. Use the function-centered plots to investigate those possibilities, then return to the pooled profile for context. The two levels describe related parts of the same community, rather than identical measurements.
